source: Nickles (ed.) (1980) Scientific Discovery: Case Studies, and Scientific Discovery, Logic, and Rationality (Boston Studies, Reidel)
finding: Two companion Reidel volumes. One holds case studies, one holds logic and rationality essays. They revived the claim that discovery can be studied by reasoning, not only justification. SEP lists the logic volume with essays by Curd, Koertge, Laudan.
numbers: Contents of the case volume not described on the page I opened.
limits: Case volume itself not read.
agent_relevance: Treat historical cases as logs of operator sequences. Our agent needs the sequences, not the grand theory.

source: Darden (1997) Recent Work in Computational Scientific Discovery, Proc. CogSci 19
finding: Science was recast as problem solving, so AI heuristics can be applied to historical and current discoveries. Buchanan and Simon were the pioneers. Programs give 'how possibly' accounts, not proof of what the scientist did.
numbers: KEKADA used notebook evidence and focused on responses to surprising results.
quote: modeled reasoning patterns in some discoveries of the biochemist Hans Krebs and focused on responses to surprising experimental results
limits: OCR of the PDF is noisy. Review, not primary data.
agent_relevance: Reproducing a history proves sufficiency, not necessity. Do not claim our schema is how scientists think.

source: Darden (1997) Recent Work in Computational Scientific Discovery, Proc. CogSci 19
finding: Humans fix on one hypothesis too early before searching the hypothesis space systematically. Discovery programs search more systematically and so can help scientists.
numbers: Example: MECHEM (Valdes-Perez 1994) found chemical reaction pathways that chemists had missed.
limits: Claim relayed from cognitive-science work, no effect size given.
agent_relevance: Supports a program-controlled search of alternatives (our schema keeps control in code).

source: Darden (1997) Recent Work in Computational Scientific Discovery, Proc. CogSci 19
finding: Two kinds of discovery program goals: model human cognition, or use computation to get around human limits. Systems of the second kind need not be realistic to be useful.
limits: Position paper.
agent_relevance: Our agent is the second kind: a scaffold that circumvents model limits.

source: Kulkarni & Simon (1988) The processes of scientific discovery: the strategy of experimentation, Cognitive Science 12(2)
finding: KEKADA is a production-system program that reproduces how Hans Krebs found the urea cycle in 1932. It is built from Krebs' notebooks and interview records. Its key theme is how the scientist reacts to a surprising result.
numbers: I could not open the paper (HTTP 403). Counts of experiments and heuristics are NOT recorded; the description comes from Darden and SEP, which I did open.
limits: Secondary description only. Fetch the paper before using any heuristic list.
agent_relevance: Operator sequence source: on a surprise, check it was real, look for the cause, change the plan. Maps to S6 and S9 (to verify against the paper).

source: Kulkarni & Simon (1988) KEKADA, as described in SEP
finding: SEP says KEKADA uses problem-solving heuristics to detect regularities in data sets and simulates the Krebs cycle discovery.
limits: One-sentence summary only.
agent_relevance: Evidence that a small set of explicit heuristics can replay a real discovery.

source: Wikipedia: Hans Adolf Krebs (urea cycle section)
finding: In 1932 Krebs and student Kurt Henseleit at Freiburg used liver tissue slices in a Warburg manometer with ornithine and citrulline. Citrulline acted as a catalyst in making urea from ammonia and carbon dioxide. It was the first metabolic cycle found.
numbers: Background: Kossel and Dakin (1904) showed arginase splits arginine to ornithine and urea in a cell-free reaction.
limits: Encyclopedia summary, not a primary source.
agent_relevance: The case is a clean worked example: new method (tissue slices), unexpected catalytic role, then a cycle hypothesis.

source: Grasshoff & May (2003) Krebs and Henseleit lab notebooks, urea cycle reconstructed with computer models; MPIWG project page
finding: The full lab notebooks of Krebs and Henseleit survive. The project rebuilt the discovery in a program (Urea Modeler) to study how mistakes were found and fixed, and where hypotheses came from.
numbers: No step or experiment counts on the page.
limits: Project page, not the paper.
agent_relevance: Notebooks are the best log of impasse and correction; our S9 look-back should use the same data type (a trace).

source: Hanson (1958) Patterns of Discovery; SEP account of Kepler as abduction
finding: Hanson used Kepler's finding of the elliptical orbit of Mars as the model of abductive discovery. Lugg (1985) disputes that this reconstruction is historically accurate.
limits: Contested history. A rational reconstruction can differ from what the scientist did.
agent_relevance: Do not assume a clean reconstructed sequence matches the real one; log real traces.

source: Simon, Langley et al. (1981) BACON; as described by SEP
finding: BACON detects regularities such as constants or linear relations among terms in data, and can simulate Kepler's third law.
numbers: Heuristics named by SEP: constant, linear relation. Version counts not given.
limits: BACON versions and their numbers not opened.
agent_relevance: Data-driven operator set: look for constants, then products or ratios of variables.

source: Dunbar (1997, 2001) in-vivo studies of laboratories; Dunbar, Fugelsang & Stein (2007); as described by SEP
finding: Scientists fixing experimental problems take analogies from very similar domains. Those building new models take them from less similar ones. Far analogies are rare. Anomalous data and theory-consistent data are processed differently in the brain.
numbers: Figures not given on the page.
limits: Secondary description; sample sizes not recorded.
agent_relevance: Analogy (O7) should be near-domain when debugging, farther when building a new model.

source: Nersessian (1992, 1999, 2009) model-based reasoning; as described by SEP
finding: Conceptual innovation uses three kinds of model-based reasoning: analogical modeling, visual modeling, simulative modeling or thought experiment. Innovation abstracts and integrates source and target domains into a new model.
limits: Philosophical account from case studies such as Maxwell.
agent_relevance: Names three operators we can implement as slots: analogy, picture, simulate.

source: Thagard & Holyoak (1996) multi-constraint theory of analogy; as described by SEP
finding: Three constraints on analogical transfer: direct similarity, structural parallels, and the investigator's purposes.
limits: Described second-hand.
agent_relevance: When our agent picks an analogy, score it on all three, in code.

source: Majumder et al. (2024) DiscoveryBench
finding: Benchmark of 264 real discovery tasks (derived from published papers) in 6 domains plus 903 synthetic tasks. Best system scored 25% hypothesis match.
numbers: 264 real + 903 synthetic tasks; 6 domains; best score 25%.
quote: even the best system scores only 25%
limits: Data-analysis part of discovery only; no physical experiments.
agent_relevance: LLM agents are weak on discovery workflows taken from real cases.

source: Majumder et al. (2024) DiscoveryBench: failure analysis
finding: Best agent by workflow type: correlation analysis 55%, data selection 18%, summary statistics 18%; spatial analysis, pollen dating and ecological modeling 0%. By domain: biology 0%, engineering 7%, economics 25%, sociology 23%.
numbers: Best non-oracle agent, Hypothesis Matching Score.
limits: Task counts per domain not recorded here.
agent_relevance: Complex statistical workflows are the gap, not simple retrieval.

source: Majumder et al. (2024) DiscoveryBench: domain knowledge and oracle feedback
finding: Adding domain knowledge to archaeology tasks moved DataVoyager (GPT-4o) between 9.9% and 17.5% (extracted text garbles which is with knowledge; read as 9.9% without, 17.5% with). Reflexion with an oracle hypothesis-match signal and up to 3 trials was a baseline.
limits: Garbled text; small archaeology subset.
agent_relevance: A real external check plus retries helps; matches G2 and G3.

source: Majumder et al. (2024) DiscoveryBench: memorisation control
finding: A NoDataGuess baseline guesses the hypothesis from the description and goal alone, to measure recall of published results rather than discovery from data.
numbers: Baseline exists; its score not extracted.
limits: Number not read.
agent_relevance: Case-study benchmarks risk recall of the famous answer; always run a no-data control.

source: Jansen et al. (2024) DiscoveryWorld
finding: Simulated text world with 120 tasks over 8 topics x 3 difficulty levels, scored on task completion, relevant actions, and explanatory knowledge found. GPT-4o ReAct, Plan+Execute and Hypothesizer agents do poorly.
numbers: 24 tasks in main tables, 5 seeds each. Easy tasks 100 steps, normal and challenge 1000 steps.
limits: GPT-4o only for agents. Simulated, not real science.
agent_relevance: Scores process and knowledge, not only the final answer.

source: Jansen et al. (2024) DiscoveryWorld: agent results
finding: Best completion: ReAct 38% of easy and 18% of challenge tasks. Best knowledge: Hypothesizer 34% of gold knowledge on easy and 8% on challenge. Unit-test sub-skills reach about 60%+ completion.
limits: Knowledge scoring uses a GPT-4o grader.
agent_relevance: Agents can do parts (measure) but cannot chain them; the gap is control, which supports a program-run loop.

source: Jansen et al. (2024) DiscoveryWorld: human scientists
finding: Up to 11 human scientists per task seed. Average completion 66%, knowledge 55%. 11 of 16 human-played tasks had completion above 60%. When stuck, humans tried brute force, e.g. all crystal frequencies, instead of fitting a regression.
limits: Small human sample per task; some Challenge tasks solved by one person.
agent_relevance: Humans also fall into brute force when stuck; an impasse rule (S6) should force a method change.

source: Shojaee et al. (2025) LLM-SR, ICLR
finding: Treats equations as programs. LLM proposes skeletons, data fits parameters, evolutionary search loops. Beats symbolic-regression baselines, especially out of domain, with 2.5K iterations versus 2M+.
numbers: E. coli growth problem: OOD NMSE about 0.0037 vs >1 for other methods.
limits: 4 benchmark problems, built to avoid recitation.
agent_relevance: Hypothesis from the LLM, parameters and score by code: the same split as our schema.

source: Shojaee et al. (2025) LLM-SR ablation
finding: Removing the iterative refinement loop: NMSE 1.01e-1 in-domain, 1.81e-1 OOD. Removing the skeleton plus separate optimizer: 3.78e-1 and 3.75e-1. Removing the natural-language prior hurt considerably; single-line expressions hurt less.
limits: One problem.
agent_relevance: Domain knowledge and the code-run loop both matter.

source: Shojaee et al. (2025) LLM-SRBench, ICML
finding: 239 problems across four domains. LSR-Transform rewrites Feynman equations into uncommon forms; LSR-Synth uses invented problems. Best system 31.5% symbolic accuracy on Transform, 28.1% on Synth.
limits: Benchmark authors' own methods are among those compared.
agent_relevance: Famous-case results are inflated by memory.

source: Shojaee et al. (2025) LLM-SRBench: memorisation signal
finding: On Feynman problems the numeric error drops sharply and symbolic error is far lower, which the authors read as memorisation, not gradual discovery.
limits: Interpretation, not a direct test.
agent_relevance: Use altered or obscured historical cases to test reasoning.

source: Lu et al. (2024) The AI Scientist
finding: End-to-end pipeline of idea, experiment, write-up and automated review. Cost under $15 per paper. The automated reviewer correlates 0.18 with the average human score vs 0.14 between two humans.
limits: Weaker models show over-optimism bias in review.
agent_relevance: Tests the whole loop but with an LLM judge of quality (G5 warns).

source: Chen et al. (2024) ScienceAgentBench
finding: 102 tasks from 44 peer-reviewed papers. Best agent solves 32.4% alone and 34.3% with expert knowledge. OpenAI o1-preview reaches 42.2%.
limits: Tasks are data-analysis code, not new discoveries.
agent_relevance: More inference compute helps; expert hints barely do.

source: Huang et al. (2024) MLAgentBench
finding: 13 ML experimentation tasks. Best agent (Claude v3 Opus) 37.5% average success. Success ranges from 100% on old datasets to 0% on recent Kaggle ones.
limits: Newer-task failure may partly reflect missing memorised knowledge.
agent_relevance: Old famous tasks are easy; new ones are not.

source: Holmes (1980/1991) on Krebs; Gruber (1974) Darwin on Man (not opened)
finding: Holmes' notebook study of Krebs underlies KEKADA, and Gruber's notebook reconstruction of Darwin is the standard single-case study. Not opened this session.
limits: From background knowledge only; verify before use.
agent_relevance: Targets for the next pass (notebook angle).
